**Black Saint** and **Soul Note** are two affiliated [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy") [independent record labels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_record_label "Independent record label"). Since their conception in the 1970s, they have released albums from a variety of influential jazz musicians, particularly in the genre of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz").

## History

Black Saint was established in 1975 by Giacomo Pellicciotti and devoted to recording avant-garde musicians who might not have an opportunity elsewhere.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-LarkinGE-1) In 1979, a sister label, Soul Note, was established as a home for artists who, while being no less creative, might be considered slightly closer to the mainstream.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-LarkinGE-1)

The labels specialize in avant-garde jazz stemming from the free jazz tradition.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-LarkinGE-1) Some of its roster of artists were members of the Chicago-based music association [Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians") and the St. Louis-based multidisciplinary arts collectives [Black Artists Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group "Black Artists Group") and the [Human Arts Ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Arts_Ensemble "Human Arts Ensemble").

The company was based in [Tribiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribiano "Tribiano"), Italy. Many of the recordings were made in Milan, as the performers passed through the area on tour,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-2) although many leading Italian musicians, such as [Giorgio Gaslini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_Gaslini "Giorgio Gaslini"), have also recorded for the label.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-LarkinGE-1) Giovanni Bonandrini's son Flavio ran the company until its sale in 2008, the elder Bonandrini having retired, and has supervised many recording sessions in New York City.

Starting in 1984, Black Saint/Soul Note won the _[Down Beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_Beat "Down Beat")_ Critics Poll for best record label for six subsequent years until they were replaced by [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") in 1990.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-3)

Cam Jazz acquired the company in 2008.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note#cite_note-4)

Koester and the label moved to Chicago, Illinois, in 1958, and the label's name became **Delmark**. Koester sold the label assets in 2018, and the label since operates as **Delmark Records LLC.** ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Delmark_Records&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] Born in 1932 in [Wichita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita,_Kansas "Wichita, Kansas"), Kansas, [Bob Koester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Koester "Bob Koester") was the son of a petroleum engineer. While in the hospital with polio when he was a child, he listened to the radio and was cheered up when he heard [Eddie Condon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Condon "Eddie Condon") and [Benny Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Goodman "Benny Goodman"). In his teens, he was a dedicated jazz fan who began buying old records from a Salvation Army store. At concerts in Kansas City, he heard [Red Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Allen "Red Allen"), [Count Basie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Basie "Count Basie"), [Jimmy Rushing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Rushing "Jimmy Rushing"), [Tommy Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Douglas_(clarinetist) "Tommy Douglas (clarinetist)"), [Lionel Hampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Hampton "Lionel Hampton"), and [Jay McShann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_McShann "Jay McShann").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records#cite_note-Kennedy-2) Moving from Wichita to St. Louis to attend college, Koester began his career as a record trader in his dormitory room. Joining a local jazz club gave Koester his first taste of live jazz, seeing [Clark Terry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Terry "Clark Terry") perform. Koester made acquaintance with a fellow jazz club member, Ron Fister, with whom he opened his first record shop, K & F Sales. Shortly after opening in an old restaurant storefront, they changed the name to the Blue Note Record Shop. About a year after this joint venture, Fister and Koester decided to part ways, with Koester moving to the corner of Delmar and Olive streets in St. Louis. Taking the name from the street his shop was on, Koester recorded a local jazz group the Windy City Six in 1953. Shortly thereafter, Koester found local talent such as [James Crutchfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Crutchfield "James Crutchfield"), [Speckled Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speckled_Red "Speckled Red"), [J.D. Short](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J.D._Short "J.D. Short"), and [Big Joe Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Joe_Williams "Big Joe Williams"). Koester moved to Chicago in August 1958. He bought Seymour's Jazz Mart, and in renaming the storefront the Jazz Record Mart, Delmark Records found its new home in the basement of the record shop. By 1963, Koester had moved the shop to a location at 7 West Grand. During this period in Chicago, Delmark released albums by, [Barney Bigard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barney_Bigard "Barney Bigard"), [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd"), [Jimmy Forrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Forrest_(musician) "Jimmy Forrest (musician)"), [George Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lewis_(clarinetist) "George Lewis (clarinetist)"), [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell"), and [Ira Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ira_Sullivan "Ira Sullivan"). Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, Delmark recorded the [Art Ensemble of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago "Art Ensemble of Chicago"), [Sonny Stitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Stitt "Sonny Stitt"), [Junior Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_Wells "Junior Wells"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records#cite_note-3) [Luther Allison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luther_Allison "Luther Allison"), [Arthur Crudup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Crudup "Arthur Crudup"), [Jimmy Dawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Dawkins "Jimmy Dawkins"), [Sleepy John Estes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_John_Estes "Sleepy John Estes"), [Buddy Guy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Guy "Buddy Guy"), [J. | Professional ratings _**Outward Bound**_ is the debut [album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album "Album") by [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") multi-instrumentalist [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy"), released in 1960. It is oriented towards straight [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), and slightly less adventurous than the majority of his later recordings.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-Simosko44-4) The album was recorded at [Van Gelder Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Gelder_Studio "Van Gelder Studio") in New Jersey and features Dolphy in a quintet with trumpeter [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), pianist [Jaki Byard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaki_Byard "Jaki Byard"), bassist [George Tucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Tucker_(musician) "George Tucker (musician)") and drummer [Roy Haynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Haynes "Roy Haynes"). Hubbard had shared living space with Dolphy when they both first arrived in New York City.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-5) The cover artwork was by Dolphy's friend [Richard "Prophet" Jennings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Slater_Jennings "Richard Slater Jennings").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-6) Of the three Dolphy originals on the album, "G.W." is dedicated to the [Californian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") bandleader [Gerald Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Wilson "Gerald Wilson"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-Simosko44-4) "Les" is named after the [trombonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombone "Trombone") Lester Robertson,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-payne-7) and "245" was the number of Dolphy's house on Carlton Avenue, in Brooklyn's [Fort Greene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Greene,_Brooklyn "Fort Greene, Brooklyn") neighborhood.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-8) ## Reception \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Reception")\] Jazz critic [Martin Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Williams_(writer) "Martin Williams (writer)") wrote: "From the first selection on Dolphy's first album under his own name... it was obvious that fresh and important talent had arrived."[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-9) _[All About Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_About_Jazz "All About Jazz")_ reviewer Douglas Payne described the album as "an ardently passionate gathering with pristine contributions from some of jazz's most flexible avatars... The music ranks, perhaps, as some of Dolphy's most accessible and most easily enjoyed."[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-payne-7) Regarding "G.W.", J. Hunter wrote: "While the rest of the band lays down beats and fills that would not be out of place on any bop date, Dolphy steps out of the head to blister us with a mind-boggling, lightning-fingered alto solo that threatens to go over a cliff at any moment. _Find sources:_ ["Musica Elettronica Viva"](https://www.google.com/search?as_eq=wikipedia&q=%22Musica+Elettronica+Viva%22)– [news](https://www.google.com/search?tbm=nws&q=%22Musica+Elettronica+Viva%22+-wikipedia&tbs=ar:1) **·** [newspapers](https://www.google.com/search?&q=%22Musica+Elettronica+Viva%22&tbs=bkt:s&tbm=bks) **·** [books](https://www.google.com/search?tbs=bks:1&q=%22Musica+Elettronica+Viva%22+-wikipedia) **·** [scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Musica+Elettronica+Viva%22) **·** [JSTOR](https://www.jstor.org/action/doBasicSearch?Query=%22Musica+Elettronica+Viva%22&acc=on&wc=on)_(December 2010)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | **Musica Elettronica Viva** (MEV) is a live acoustic/electronic improvisational group formed in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), in 1966. Defined as "something of an irregular institution, a band that has come together intermittently through the years",[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-Perkis-1994-1) Musica Elettronica Viva's founding members were Allan Bryant, [Alvin Curran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Curran "Alvin Curran"), Jon Phetteplace and [Frederic Rzewski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_Rzewski "Frederic Rzewski"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-2) [Richard Teitelbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Teitelbaum "Richard Teitelbaum"),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-Perkis-1994-1) and [Carol Plantamura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Plantamura "Carol Plantamura").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-3) Other members include [Ivan Vandor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Vandor "Ivan Vandor") and [Steve Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lacy_(saxophonist) "Steve Lacy (saxophonist)").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-4) [Garrett List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrett_List "Garrett List") and [George E. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Lewis "George E. Lewis") subsequently joined the group.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-Perkis-1994-1) Musica Elettronica Viva were early experimenters in the use of synthesizers. A 1967 performance in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") featured a rendition of [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage")'s _Solo for Voice 2_ with Plantamura's voice transformed through a [Moog synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_synthesizer "Moog synthesizer"). At the end of the 1960s, they took part in the group [Lo Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lo_Zoo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lo Zoo"), founded by artist [Michelangelo Pistoletto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelangelo_Pistoletto "Michelangelo Pistoletto"). They also used such "non-musical" objects as amplified panes of glass and motor oil cans. Their performances achieved mainstream notoriety in Italy for generating vocal audience participation, occasionally resulting in riots, for example at the Musee d'Art Moderne in Paris, at Queen Anne's Hall in London where the police and the fire department kicked the group out, and at the Teatro Regio in Parma where the authorities shut the house lights down and emptied the hall, inspiring a street demonstration led by Jean-Jacques Lebel. Musica Elettronica Viva disbanded in 2017 after a final tour, though at least two CDs were released subsequently. Among the many who performed with the group, Jon Phetteplace died decades ago, Steve Lacy in 2004, Maryanne Amacher in 2009, Garrett List in 2019, Ivan Vandor and Richard Teitelbaum in 2020, and Frederic Rzewski in 2021.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva#cite_note-5) ## Discography - _Spacecraft_, recorded in Cologne in 1967 by Bryant, Curran, Rzewski, Teitelbaum and Vandor - _Unified Patchwork Theory_, recorded in Zurich in 1990 by Curran, Rzewski, Teitelbaum, Steve Lacy, and [Garrett List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrett_List "Garrett List") Both of the above first issued in 2001 on CD as "Spacecraft/Unified Patchwork Theory" (Alga Marghen, Plana-M 15NMN.038). - _Friday_, recorded in London in 1969 by Curran, Rzewski, Teitelbaum, Franco Cataldi and Gunther Carius, reissued 2008 (ALGA 073CD) - _The Sound Pool_, recorded 1969, reissued 1998 (Spalax CD14969) - _United Patchwork_, recorded November 1977 in Rome by Curran, Rzewski, Teitelbaum, Lacy, List, and [Karl Berger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Berger "Karl Berger") (Horo 2xLP HDP 15-16) - _MEV 40_, recorded 1967–2007, a 4-CD set of previously unpublished performances issued by [New World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World_Records "New World Records") in 2008 (CD80675) - _Apogee_, a double CD (Matchless Recordings, MRCD61, 2005) shared with another of the electronic improvisational ensembles that emerged during the 1960s: [AMM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMM_(group) "AMM (group)"). The first CD is a studio recording in a joint session in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") on April 30, 2004 featuring MEV's Curran, Teitelbaum and Rzewski with the three members of [AMM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMM_(group) "AMM (group)"). This is the first occasion that the two ensembles have performed together, but not the first time they have shared a split release - each outfit filled a side of the LP Live Electronic Music Improvised, released on a US label (Mainstream) in 1968. The second CD consists of the performances that each group gave at a festival held in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") on May 1, 2004. - Symphony No 106, Les Disques Victo, 2016 VICTO CD 129, 2016, and digital album - Symphony No. 105, a Café Oto download available as 320k MP3 or 24bit FLAC, 2016 - Symphony No 108, Live at Brno Philharmonic, Hermes' Ear - HE CD 015 / aSB 03, 2017 - Spacecraft Alga Marghen CD 2001, Our Swimmer LP, welle 104LP, 2021 - Symphony No. 107 - The Bard, Black Truffle 104, June 2023 ## References 1. # Globe Unity Orchestra Globe Unity Orchestra Free jazz ensemble The **Globe Unity Orchestra** is a [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") ensemble. Globe Unity was formed in autumn 1966 with a commission received by [Alexander von Schlippenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Schlippenbach "Alexander von Schlippenbach") from the [Berlin Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JazzFest_Berlin "JazzFest Berlin").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globe_Unity_Orchestra#cite_note-as-1) It had its debut at the [Berliner Philharmonie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berliner_Philharmonie "Berliner Philharmonie") on 3 November combining [Gunter Hampel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunter_Hampel "Gunter Hampel")'s quartet with [Manfred Schoof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Schoof "Manfred Schoof")' s quintet and [Peter Brötzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann "Peter Brötzmann")'s trio:[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globe_Unity_Orchestra#cite_note-2) Hampel (bcl, fl); [Willem Breuker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willem_Breuker "Willem Breuker") (bs, ss); Schoof (tp) with [Gerd Dudek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerd_Dudek "Gerd Dudek") (ts); [Alexander von Schlippenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Schlippenbach "Alexander von Schlippenbach") (p); [Buschi Niebergall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschi_Niebergall "Buschi Niebergall") (b) and [Jaki Liebezeit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaki_Liebezeit "Jaki Liebezeit") (d) on one side, Brötzmann (saxophones), [Peter Kowald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Kowald "Peter Kowald") (b, tuba), [Sven-Åke Johansson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sven-%C3%85ke_Johansson "Sven-Åke Johansson") (d) on the other. During the next years this core group was completed by other European and American musicians: [Johannes Bauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannes_Bauer "Hannes Bauer") (tb), [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton") (as, cl), [Willem Breuker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willem_Breuker "Willem Breuker") (ts), [Rüdiger Carl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%BCdiger_Carl?action=edit&redlink=1 "Rüdiger Carl") (as, ts), [Günter Christmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Christmann?action=edit&redlink=1 "Günter Christmann") (tb), [Gunter Hampel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunter_Hampel "Gunter Hampel") (bcl), [Toshinori Kondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toshinori_Kondo "Toshinori Kondo") (tp), [Steve Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lacy_(saxophonist) "Steve Lacy (saxophonist)") (ss), [Paul Lovens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Lovens "Paul Lovens") (drums), [Paul Lytton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Lytton "Paul Lytton") (drums), [Albert Mangelsdorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Mangelsdorff "Albert Mangelsdorff") (tb), [Evan Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Parker "Evan Parker") (ss, ts), [Michel Pilz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Pilz "Michel Pilz") (bcl, cl, bars), [Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst-Ludwig_Petrowsky "Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky") (as, cl, fl), [Enrico Rava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Rava "Enrico Rava") (tp), [Paul Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Rutherford_(trombonist) "Paul Rutherford (trombonist)") (tb), [Heinz Sauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinz_Sauer "Heinz Sauer") (ss, ts), [Bob Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Stewart_(musician) "Bob Stewart (musician)") (tuba), [Tomasz Stańko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomasz_Sta%C5%84ko "Tomasz Stańko") (tp), and [Kenny Wheeler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Wheeler "Kenny Wheeler") (tp). The Orchestra has been described as providing "the most remarkable assemblies of outside jazz talent since the AACM big bands".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globe_Unity_Orchestra#cite_note-3) They performed in New Delhi, India for the Jazz Yatra in late 1970s. They performed at the Ashoka Hotel, New Delhi in 1978. The final concert in the group's main lifetime was at the [Chicago Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Jazz_Festival "Chicago Jazz Festival") in 1987.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globe_Unity_Orchestra#cite_note-as-1) The 40th anniversary line-up for the 2006 concerts and recordings were the saxophone players Evan Parker, Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky, Gerd Dudek, [Rudi Mahall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudi_Mahall "Rudi Mahall") (bcl), the trumpets Kenny Wheeler, Manfred Schoof, Axel Dörner, Jean-Luc Cappozzo and trombonists Paul Rutherford, [George E. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Lewis "George E. Lewis"), [Jeb Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bishop "Jeb Bishop"), J. # European free jazz European free jazz Music genre | | | | --- | --- | | ![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f2/Edit-clear.svg/120px-Edit-clear.svg.png) | This article's style of writing **may not reflect the [encyclopedic tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing_better_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles") used on Wikipedia**. See Wikipedia's [guide to writing better articles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing_better_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles") for suggestions._(May 2026)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/39/Bailey1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bailey1.jpg) [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)") **European free jazz** is a part of the global [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") scene with its own development and characteristics. It is hard to establish who are the founders of European free jazz because of the different developments in different European countries. One can, however, make an argument that European free jazz took its development from American [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), where musicians such as [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") revolutionised the way of playing. As the British drummer [Eddie Prévost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Pr%C3%A9vost "Eddie Prévost"), of long-standing improvising ensemble AMM, has put it, 'the music of Ornette Coleman and Albert Ayler gave us _permission to disobey_.'[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-1) Yet at much the same time, there were significant European innovations: for example, the same year as Coleman's [_Free Jazz_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation") album was released (1961), in the UK the Jamaican alto saxophonist [Joe Harriott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Harriott "Joe Harriott") released the first of his experimental albums, _[Free Form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Form_(Joe_Harriott_album) "Free Form (Joe Harriott album)")._ It was recorded in late 1960, the month before Coleman's.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-2) ## American origin Free jazz got its name from the album _Free Jazz_ (Atlantic, 1961) by Ornette Coleman to describe American avant-garde jazz of the 1960s.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3) Besides "avant-garde", it was called "the New Wave", "the New Thing", "action jazz", and in Europe "improvised music".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3) Germans played a form of free jazz that had something in common with the [aleatoric music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleatoric_music "Aleatoric music") of [Bernd Alois Zimmermann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernd_Alois_Zimmermann "Bernd Alois Zimmermann") and was performed by [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)"), [Joachim Kuhn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_Kuhn "Joachim Kuhn"), [Albert Mangelsdorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Mangelsdorff "Albert Mangelsdorff"), [Manfred Schoof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Schoof "Manfred Schoof"), [John Surman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Surman "John Surman"), and [Alexander von Schlippenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Schlippenbach "Alexander von Schlippenbach").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3) Free jazz was unpopular and didn't sell well.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3) It was viewed as a musical, political, and social backlash to the structure of jazz and of American society at the time. "For some performers the style was loosely linked to the [Black Power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Power "Black Power") movement in the USA, partly because of the radical political outlook of some of its practitioners and advocates (e.g., [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp") and [LeRoi Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeRoi_Jones "LeRoi Jones") – later known as Amiri Baraka) and partly owing to the explosive, expressionistic nature of the music itself".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-4) Due to the lack of commercial success of the free jazz music as well as the racial issues, like the [Civil Rights Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Movement "Civil Rights Movement"), many American free jazz musicians began touring the European continent, playing and spreading their new avant-garde style throughout Europe.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-autogenerated1-5) Jazz musicians like Ornette Coleman, [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell"), [Don Byas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Byas "Don Byas") traveled and performed throughout Europe.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-6) In contrast to the lack of commercial success in America, many American free jazz musicians experienced both commercial success and acceptance in Europe, leading to tours of Europe and extended residencies.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-7) "A number of jazz musicians migrated to other parts of the world, where they received an opposite response, being considered the ultimate expression of high culture. Thus, many of them remained in exile, and they enjoyed unparalleled success in France, Germany, Japan, Scandinavia, and the Netherlands after the world wars".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-8) Although much of American public believed this music to be structure-less, provocative, and ridiculous, some European listeners enjoyed the "dissonant and seemingly chaotic music".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-9) "Many Europeans viewed free jazz as the descriptor most used by the media on both sides of the Atlantic for a musical movement that ignited like a flare in the African-American... and Western European...jazz communities. The social context in both cases included a reaction by musicians against a mainstream jazz culture they felt to be colluding with an oppressive Western hegemony that was intrinsically racist, historically imperialistic and exploitive, venally decadent and vicious as its power was challenged".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-10) Due in part to the provocative nature of the music as well as the freedom it granted both the musician and the listener, many Europeans associated the backlash toward American society conveyed in free jazz with the [counter-culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture_of_the_1960s "Counterculture of the 1960s") and anti-imperialist movements in Europe during the late 1960s. ## European acceptance Contrary to the societal reaction free jazz music received in the United States, many Europeans (musicians, critics and young people alike) identified with this style of music. While many African-Americans associated this avant-garde style with the Civil Rights Movement in America, many Europeans in the 1960s, especially college-aged students, associated this style of music with anti-colonialist movements occurring throughout Europe at the same time. [Los Angeles, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles,_California "Los Angeles, California"), U.S. | | Genre | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") | | Occupations | Musician, composer | | Instruments | Piano, trombone | | Years active | 1950s–1990s | | Label | [Arabesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabesque_Records "Arabesque Records") | Musical artist **Horace Elva Tapscott** (April 6, 1934– February 27, 1999) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") pianist and composer.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-amg-1) He formed the Pan Afrikan Peoples Arkestra (also known as P.A.P.A., or The Ark) in 1961 and led the ensemble through the 1990s.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-ucla-bio-2) ## Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life")\] Tapscott was born in [Houston, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas"), and moved to [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), at the age of nine.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) By this time he had begun to study piano and trombone.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) He played with [Frank Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Morgan_(musician) "Frank Morgan (musician)"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), Bobby Bradford, and [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins") as a teenager. ## Later life and career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Later life and career")\] After service in the [Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") in [Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming "Wyoming"), he returned to Los Angeles and played trombone with various bands, notably [Lionel Hampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Hampton "Lionel Hampton") (1959–61). Soon after, though, he quit playing trombone and focused on piano.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-Grove-4) In 1961, Tapscott formed the Pan Afrikan Peoples Arkestra,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-5) with the aim of preserving, developing and performing African-American music. As his vision grew, this became just one part of a larger organization in 1963, the Underground Musicians Association (UGMA),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) which later changed name to the [Union of God's Musicians and Artists Ascension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_God's_Musicians_and_Artists_Ascension "Union of God's Musicians and Artists Ascension") (UGMAA).[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-Grove-4) [Arthur Blythe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blythe "Arthur Blythe"), [Stanley Crouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Crouch "Stanley Crouch"), [Butch Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butch_Morris "Butch Morris"), [Wilber Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilber_Morris "Wilber Morris"), [David Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Murray_(saxophonist) "David Murray (saxophonist)"), [Jimmy Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Woods "Jimmy Woods"), [Nate Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nate_Morgan "Nate Morgan") and [Guido Sinclair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_Sinclair "Guido Sinclair") all performed in Tapscott's Arkestra at one time or another.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-ucla-bio-2) Tapscott and his work are the subjects of the [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles") Horace Tapscott Jazz Collection.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-oac-6) Enthusiasts of his music formed two labels in the 1970s and 1980s, Interplay and Nimbus, for which he recorded.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-Grove-4) From [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"): "His pianistic technique was hard and percussive, likened by some to that of [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk") and [Herbie Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Nichols "Herbie Nichols") and every bit as distinctive. In contexts ranging from freely improvised duos to highly arranged big bands, Tapscott exhibited a solo and compositional voice that was his own." ## Death and legacy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Death and legacy")\] Having been suffering from brain cancer, Tapscott died aged 64 on February 27, 1999, the day before a planned tribute concert in his honor took place at Los Angeles' [Leimert Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leimert_Park,_Los_Angeles "Leimert Park, Los Angeles").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-7) An engraving in the sidewalk along Degnan Boulevard in the Leimert Park neighborhood reads: "Horace Tapscott, the local pianist and organizer whose ensemble, the Pan Afrikan Peoples Arkestra, gave many musicians their first gigs and helped heal a community impacted by racism."[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-8) His personal archive of manuscripts, arrangements and recordings was donated to [UCLA Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA_Library "UCLA Library") in 2003 by his wife, Cecilia Tapscott.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-9) ## Discography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Discography")\] ### As leader \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=5 "Edit section: As leader")\] - Over a career spanning more than six decades, he received 12 [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") and the [Polar Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_Music_Prize "Polar Music Prize"), and was acclaimed worldwide for his originality, compositional depth, and transformative approach to [musical improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-grammy-ws-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-chow-2) Shorter first rose to mainstream prominence in 1959 after joining [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey")'s [Jazz Messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Messengers "Jazz Messengers"), where he quickly became the ensemble's primary composer and one of its defining creative voices. In 1964, he joined [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s [Second Great Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet#Second_Great_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet"), contributing compositions and performances that helped shape one of the most innovative and influential periods in jazz history. In 1970, he co-founded the [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") band [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report"), which achieved international success and redefined the possibilities of electric jazz. As a bandleader, Shorter recorded more than 20 albums, and many of his compositions—including works written for Davis, Weather Report, and his own groups—became enduring [jazz standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"). His music is noted for its harmonic sophistication, narrative structure, and philosophical depth, earning sustained critical praise and influence across generations of musicians. Shorter was especially acclaimed for his mastery of the [soprano saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano_saxophone "Soprano saxophone"), having shifted his primary focus from the [tenor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone") in the late 1960s. Beginning in 1970, he dominated _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine's annual critics' and readers' polls on soprano saxophone, winning the critics' poll for 10 consecutive years and the readers' poll for 18.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-3) In 2008, _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ music critic [Ben Ratliff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Ratliff "Ben Ratliff") described Shorter as "probably jazz's greatest living small-group composer and a contender for greatest living improviser," a characterization that reflected his towering status within the genre.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-Ratliff-4) ## Early life and education \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")\] Wayne Shorter was born in [Newark, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark,_New_Jersey "Newark, New Jersey"),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-Larkin-5) the son of Louise and Joseph Shorter.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-6) He graduated from [Newark Arts High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark_Arts_High_School "Newark Arts High School")[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-8) in 1952. Encouraged by his parents, Shorter began taking [clarinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarinet "Clarinet") lessons at age 16 and later switched to [tenor saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone"). While in high school, Wayne performed with the Nat Phipps Band in Newark. His older brother [Alan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Shorter "Alan Shorter") played [alto saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_saxophone "Alto saxophone") before switching to the [trumpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trumpet "Trumpet") in college. Shorter enrolled at [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University") in 1952 and graduated with a degree in [music education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_education "Music education") in 1956. After graduating, Shorter spent two years in the [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army"), during which time he played briefly with [Horace Silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Silver "Horace Silver"). After his discharge, he played with [Maynard Ferguson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maynard_Ferguson "Maynard Ferguson"). While growing up, Shorter loved comic books and science fiction as well as music. In his youth, Shorter acquired the nickname "Mr. Gone", which later became an album title for Weather Report.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter#cite_note-9) ## Career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wayne_Shorter&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Career")\] | | | | --- | --- | [... middle omitted — see footer ...] - [The Jazz Messengers members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:The_Jazz_Messengers_members "Category:The Jazz Messengers members") - [V.S.O.P. # Music genre Music genre Classification of music by tradition or style A **music genre** is a conventional category that identifies some pieces of [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music") as belonging to a shared tradition or set of conventions.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-1) [Genre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genre "Genre") is to be distinguished from [musical form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_form "Musical form") and **musical style**, although in practice these terms are sometimes used interchangeably.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-2) Music can be divided into genres in numerous ways, sometimes broadly and with polarity, e.g., [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music") as opposed to [art music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music") or [folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), or, as another example, [religious music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_music "Religious music") and [secular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secular_music "Secular music"). Often, however, classification draws on the proliferation of derivative subgenres, fusion genres, and [microgenres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microgenre "Microgenre") that has started to accrue, e.g., [screamo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screamo "Screamo"), [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop"), and [mumble rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumble_rap "Mumble rap"), respectively. The artistic nature of music means that these classifications are often subjective and controversial, and some may overlap. As genres evolve, novel music is sometimes lumped into existing categories. ## Definitions Douglass M. Green distinguishes between genre and [form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_form "Musical form") in his 1965 book _Form in Tonal Music_. He lists [madrigal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrigal_(music) "Madrigal (music)"), [motet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motet "Motet"), [canzona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canzona "Canzona"), [ricercar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricercar "Ricercar"), and dance as examples of genres from the [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_music "Renaissance music") period. To further clarify the meaning of _genre_, Green writes about " [Beethoven's Op. 61](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_Concerto_(Beethoven) "Violin Concerto (Beethoven)")" and "Mendelssohn's Op. 64 ". He explains that both are identical in genre and are [violin concertos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violin_concerto "Violin concerto") that have different forms. However, Mozart's Rondo for Piano, K. 511, and the _Agnus Dei_ from his Mass, K. 317, are quite different in genre but happen to be similar in form."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-3) In 1982, [Franco Fabbri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco_Fabbri "Franco Fabbri") proposed a definition of the musical genre that is now considered to be normative:[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-Moore-4) "musical genre is a set of musical events (real or possible) whose course is governed by a definite set of socially accepted rules", where a musical event can be defined as "any type of activity performed around any type of event involving sound".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-:2-5) A music genre or subgenre may be defined by the [musical techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_technique "Musical technique"), the cultural context, and the content and spirit of the themes. Geographical origin is sometimes used to identify a music genre, though a single geographical category will often include a wide variety of subgenres. Timothy Laurie argues that, since the early 1980s, "genre has graduated from being a subset of popular music studies to being an almost ubiquitous framework for constituting and evaluating musical research objects".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-6) The term _genre_ is generally defined similarly by many authors and musicologists, while the related term _style_ has different interpretations and definitions. Some, like [Peter van der Merwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_van_der_Merwe_(musicologist) "Peter van der Merwe (musicologist)"), treat the terms _genre_ and _style_ as the same, saying that _genre_ should be defined as pieces of music that share a certain style or "basic musical language".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-Pete-7) Others, such as Allan F. Moore, state that _genre_ and _style_ are two separate terms, and that secondary characteristics such as subject matter can also differentiate between genres.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-Moore-4) ### Subtypes "Fusion genre" redirects here. For fusion genres in literary and film works, see [Hybrid genre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_genre "Hybrid genre"). See also: [Category:Fusion music genres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Fusion_music_genres "Category:Fusion music genres") A _[subgenre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subgenre "Subgenre")_ is a [subordinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierarchy "Hierarchy") within a genre.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-9) In music terms, it is a subcategory of a musical genre that adopts its basic characteristics, but also has its own set of characteristics that clearly distinguish and set it apart within the genre. A subgenre is also sometimes referred to as a style within the genre.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-12) The proliferation of popular music in the 20th century has led to over 1,200 definable subgenres of music. A musical composition may be situated in the intersection of two or more genres, sharing characteristics of each [parent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superior_(hierarchy) "Superior (hierarchy)") genre, and therefore belong to each of them at the same time.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-:2-5) Such subgenres are known as _fusion genres_.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Examples of fusion genres include [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"), which is a fusion of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") and rock music, and [country rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_rock "Country rock") which is a fusion of [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") and rock music. A _[microgenre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microgenre "Microgenre")_ is a niche genre,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre#cite_note-13) as well as a subcategory within major genres or their subgenres. ## Categorization and emergence of new genres The [genealogy of musical genres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genealogy_of_musical_genres "Genealogy of musical genres") expresses, often in the form of a written chart. New genres of music can arise through the development of new styles of music; in addition to simply creating a new categorization. Although it is conceivable to create a musical style with no relation to existing genres, new styles usually appear under the influence of pre-existing genres. - [Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") | | Cultural origins | 1970s, United States | | Fusion genres | | [Crossover jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossover_jazz "Crossover jazz") | | Other topics | | [List of musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_smooth_jazz_musicians "List of smooth jazz musicians") | **Smooth jazz** is a commercially oriented sub-genre style of jazz music by R&B, funk, rock and pop music styles (separately, or in any combination). Beginning in the early-1970s, [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") (aka "fusion") was a movement by some jazz musicians to merge the instrumental virtuosity and improvisation of traditional jazz, with a modern, electronic sensibility. The instrument that has become the most widely-associated with the genre is the saxophone inspired by players like [Grover Washington Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Washington_Jr. "Grover Washington Jr."), [Ronnie Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Laws "Ronnie Laws"), [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") and [Nathan Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Davis_(saxophonist) "Nathan Davis (saxophonist)"); plus a gentle, [legato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legato "Legato") [electric guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar") (influenced by players like [Wes Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wes_Montgomery "Wes Montgomery") and [Grant Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Green "Grant Green")). Jazz fusion ensembles such as [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report"), [Spyro Gyra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyro_Gyra "Spyro Gyra"), [Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_(band) "Hiroshima (band)") and [Bob James' Fourplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_James_(musician) "Bob James (musician)") were vital to the development of the genre. Modern derivatives of the genre includes the more recent New Adult Contemporary format broadcast radio. "Smooth jazz" has been successful as a radio format; however in 2007, the popularity of the format began to decline. Consequently, it was abandoned by several high-profile radio stations across the U.S.A., perhaps notably in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"). Many industry insiders have speculated that the smooth jazz format may die out, particularly with the industry giant [Clear Channel Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clear_Channel_Communications "Clear Channel Communications") dropping the genre. Critics of the company, however, blame Clear Channel for the format's decline, citing too much repetition of a sharply-reduced number of tracks on Clear Channel–owned stations that alienated many listeners. Despite the format's demise on commercial radio, a growing number of non-commercial stations have taken up the music. In addition, smooth jazz concerts, recording sales – as well as increased smooth jazz offerings on the Internet – continue to show strong fan support for the genre. ## Description In general, a smooth jazz track is downtempo (the most widely played tracks are in the 90–105 BPM range), layering a lead, melody-playing instrument (saxophones – especially soprano and tenor – are the most popular with guitars a close second) over a backdrop that typically consists of programmed rhythms and various pads and/or samples. Smooth jazz groups or recording artists tend to play their instruments in a melodic fashion such that they are recognizable within just a few measures; this category includes names such as saxophonists [Kenny G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_G "Kenny G"), [Najee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Najee "Najee"), [David Sanborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Sanborn "David Sanborn"), [George Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Howard_(jazz) "George Howard (jazz)") and [Art Porter Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Porter_Jr. "Art Porter Jr."); guitarists [George Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Benson "George Benson"), [Earl Klugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Klugh "Earl Klugh"), [Marc Antoine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Antoine_(musician) "Marc Antoine (musician)"), [Peter White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_White_(musician) "Peter White (musician)"), [Jonathan Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Butler "Jonathan Butler"), [Norman Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Brown_(guitarist) "Norman Brown (guitarist)"), [Ronny Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronny_Jordan "Ronny Jordan"), and [Yves Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Vincent "Yves Vincent"); keyboardist/pianists [Joe Sample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Sample "Joe Sample"), [David Benoit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Benoit "David Benoit"), and [Bradley Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradley_Joseph "Bradley Joseph"). Some performers, such as [Dave Koz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Koz "Dave Koz"), Bob James, and [Nathan East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_East "Nathan East") are notable for their numerous collaborations with many of the genre's big names. Groups include [Fourplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourplay "Fourplay"), [Pieces of a Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pieces_of_a_Dream_(band) "Pieces of a Dream (band)"), [Acoustic Alchemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_Alchemy "Acoustic Alchemy"), [Airbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbourne_(band) "Airbourne (band)") and [the Rippingtons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rippingtons "The Rippingtons"). Female performers includes [Keiko Matsui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keiko_Matsui "Keiko Matsui"), [Joyce Cooling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyce_Cooling "Joyce Cooling"), [Mindi Abair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindi_Abair "Mindi Abair"), [Candy Dulfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candy_Dulfer "Candy Dulfer"), [Sade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sade_(band) "Sade (band)"), [Brenda Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brenda_Russell "Brenda Russell"), [Pamela Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamela_Williams "Pamela Williams"), [Regina Belle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regina_Belle "Regina Belle") and [Anita Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Baker "Anita Baker"). ## History [... middle omitted — see footer ...] | Related topics | - [Adult contemporary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_contemporary_music "Adult contemporary music")

[Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), one of the pioneers of jazz-funk | | Stylistic origins | - [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz")

- [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") | | Cultural origins | Late 1960s – 1970s, United States | | Subgenres | | [Free funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_funk "Free funk") | | Other topics | | [Jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"), [rare groove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rare_groove "Rare groove") | **Jazz-funk** is a subgenre of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") music characterized by a strong [back beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music) "Beat (music)"), electrified sounds,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-1) and [analog synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_synthesizers "Analog synthesizers"). The integration of [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), [soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"), and [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") music and styles into jazz resulted in the creation of a genre that ranges from pure [jazz improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation#Jazz_improvisation "Musical improvisation") to soul, funk or [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco "Disco") with jazz arrangements, jazz [riffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff"), jazz solos, and sometimes soul vocals.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-allmusic-2) Similar genres to jazz funk include [acid jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_jazz "Acid jazz").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-3) ## History Jazz-funk generally exhibits a simple structure based around one or two riffs, and a harmonic structure that allows musicians to improvise.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-4) Modern jazz funk music was influenced by [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-5) The [Mizell Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mizell_Brothers "Mizell Brothers") were producers for many jazz and soul artists. Examples of early jazz funk albums include [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")' _[On the Corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner "On the Corner")_ (1972)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-6) and [Jimmy Smith's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Smith_(musician) "Jimmy Smith (musician)") _[Root Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_Down_(album) "Root Down (album)")_ (1972).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-7) [The Last Poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Poets "The Last Poets"), [Gil Scott-Heron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Scott-Heron "Gil Scott-Heron"), [Lightnin' Rod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightnin'_Rod "Lightnin' Rod"),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-8) [T.S. Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T.S._Monk "T.S. Monk"), [Pleasure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleasure_(Oregon_band) "Pleasure (Oregon band)"), [Boogaloo Joe Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boogaloo_Joe_Jones "Boogaloo Joe Jones"), [Lenny White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenny_White "Lenny White"), [Don Blackman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Blackman "Don Blackman"), [Monk Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monk_Higgins "Monk Higgins"), [Wilbur Bascomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Bascomb "Wilbur Bascomb"),[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-9) the Blackbyrds, [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd") and [Les DeMerle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_DeMerle "Les DeMerle")[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-10) and [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson")[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-11) released jazz funk albums. Jazz funk musicians used electric instruments, such as the [Rhodes Piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Piano "Rhodes Piano") or electric guitar, [bass guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar"), organ, particularly in [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-12) Herbie Hancock played ARP Odyssey synthesizer and [clavinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavinet "Clavinet") on album _[Head Hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters "Head Hunters")_ (1973).[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-13) The controversy\[ _[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] may have helped jazz find a larger audience.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-14) By contrast, pop audiences found it "too jazzy" and, therefore, too complex.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-15) Some mainstream artists in [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") used specialist producers to commercial success. Larry and Fonce Mizell[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-16) produced jazz-funk artists such as [Johnny "Hammond" Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_%22Hammond%22_Smith "Johnny \"Hammond\" Smith"), [Gary Bartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Bartz "Gary Bartz"), Roger Glenn, the Blackbyrds, and [Donald Byrd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Byrd "Donald Byrd").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-17) ## UK jazz funk See also: [Brit funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brit_funk "Brit funk") In the UK's nightclubs of the mid-late 1970s, DJs including [Colin Curtis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Curtis_(DJ) "Colin Curtis (DJ)") in [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester"), [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham")'s Graham Warr and [Shaun Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaun_Williams_(DJ) "Shaun Williams (DJ)"), and [Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds "Leeds")-based Ian Dewhirst and Paul Schofield championed the genre, along with [Chris Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hill_(DJ) "Chris Hill (DJ)") and Bob Jones in the South.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk#cite_note-18) London-based jazz funk pioneers drew a new audience to jazz: notably [pirate radio stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirate_radio "Pirate radio") Invicta 92.4 and JFM. - [space rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_rock "Space rock") | **Progressive rock** (shortened to **prog rock** or simply **prog**) is a broad [genre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre "Music genre") of [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music")[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartin199871%E2%80%9375-9) that primarily developed in the United States and United Kingdom through the mid- to late 1960s. Initially termed " [progressive pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_pop "Progressive pop")", the style emerged from [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music") bands who abandoned standard [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") or [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") traditions in favour of [instrumental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumentation_(music) "Instrumentation (music)") and [compositional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_(music) "Composition (music)") techniques more commonly associated with [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), or [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"), while retaining the instrumentation typical of rock music. Additional elements contributed to its " [progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music "Progressive music")" label: lyrics were more poetic, technology was harnessed for new sounds, music approached the condition of " [art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music")", and the studio, rather than the stage, [became the focus of musical activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_studio_as_an_instrument "Recording studio as an instrument"), which often involved creating music for listening rather than dancing. Progressive rock includes a fusion of styles, approaches and genres, and tends to be diverse and [eclectic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclecticism_in_music "Eclecticism in music"). Progressive rock is often associated with long solos, extended pieces, fantastic lyrics, grandiose stage sets and costumes, and an obsessive dedication to technical skill and [virtuosity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtuoso "Virtuoso"). While the genre is often cited for its merging of [high culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_culture "High culture") and [low culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_culture "Low culture"), few artists incorporated Western classical themes in their work to a significant degree, with only a minority of groups ( [Emerson, Lake & Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson,_Lake_&_Palmer "Emerson, Lake & Palmer"), [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_(band) "Renaissance (band)"), [Ekseption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekseption "Ekseption"), etc.) directly emulating or referencing classical music. - [soft rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_rock "Soft rock") | **Hard rock** or **heavy rock**[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-1) is a heavier subgenre of [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") typified by vocals and electric guitars that are aggressive and distorted relative to traditional rock music. Hard rock began in the mid-1960s with the [garage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garage_rock "Garage rock"), [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock"), and [blues rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues_rock "Blues rock") movements. Some of the earliest hard rock music was produced by [the Kinks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Kinks "The Kinks"), [the Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Who "The Who"), [the Yardbirds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Yardbirds "The Yardbirds"), [the Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones"), [Cream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cream_(band) "Cream (band)"), [Vanilla Fudge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla_Fudge "Vanilla Fudge"), and [the Jimi Hendrix Experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jimi_Hendrix_Experience "The Jimi Hendrix Experience"). In the late 1960s, bands such as [Blue Cheer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Cheer "Blue Cheer"), [the Jeff Beck Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jeff_Beck_Group "The Jeff Beck Group"), [Iron Butterfly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Butterfly "Iron Butterfly"), [Led Zeppelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Led_Zeppelin "Led Zeppelin"), [Creedence Clearwater Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creedence_Clearwater_Revival "Creedence Clearwater Revival"), [Golden Earring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Earring "Golden Earring"), [Steppenwolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steppenwolf_(band) "Steppenwolf (band)"), [Grand Funk Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Funk_Railroad "Grand Funk Railroad"), [Free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_(band) "Free (band)"), and [Deep Purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Purple "Deep Purple") also produced hard rock. The genre developed into a major form of [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music") in the 1970s, with the Who, Led Zeppelin and Deep Purple being joined by [Black Sabbath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sabbath "Black Sabbath"), [Alice Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Cooper "Alice Cooper"), [Aerosmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerosmith "Aerosmith"), [Kiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss_(band) "Kiss (band)"), [Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_(band) "Queen (band)"), [AC/DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC/DC "AC/DC"), [Thin Lizzy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thin_Lizzy "Thin Lizzy") and [Van Halen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Halen "Van Halen"). During the 1980s, some hard rock bands moved away from their hard rock roots and more towards [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-AMQueen-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock#cite_note-Bogdanov2002Queen-3) Established bands made a comeback in the mid-1980s and hard rock reached a commercial peak in the 1980s with [glam metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glam_metal "Glam metal") bands such as [Mötley Crüe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6tley_Cr%C3%BCe "Mötley Crüe"), [Bon Jovi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bon_Jovi "Bon Jovi"), [Def Leppard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Def_Leppard "Def Leppard") and [Poison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poison_(band) "Poison (band)"), as well as the rawer sounds of [Guns N' Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guns_N'_Roses "Guns N' Roses") which followed with great success in the later part of that decade. Hard rock began losing popularity with the commercial success of [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"), [urban pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_contemporary_music "Urban contemporary music"), [grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunge "Grunge"), and later [Britpop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britpop "Britpop") in the 1990s. Despite this, many [post-grunge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-grunge "Post-grunge") bands adopted a hard rock sound, and the 2000s saw renewed interest in established bands, revival attempts, and new hard rock bands. - [Chet Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Baker "Chet Baker") | Musical artist **William John Evans** (August 16, 1929 – September 15, 1980) was an American [jazz pianist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_piano "Jazz piano") and composer who worked primarily as the leader of his trio.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-2) His extensive use of [impressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism_in_music "Impressionism in music") harmony, [block chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_chord "Block chord"), innovative chord voicings, and trademark rhythmically independent "singing" melodic lines continue to influence [jazz pianists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_jazz_pianists "List of jazz pianists") today. Born in [Plainfield, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plainfield,_New_Jersey "Plainfield, New Jersey"), Evans studied classical music at [Southeastern Louisiana College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Louisiana_College "Southeastern Louisiana College") and the [Mannes School of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannes_School_of_Music "Mannes School of Music"), in New York City, where he majored in composition and received an [artist diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artist_diploma "Artist diploma"). In 1955, he moved to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), where he worked with bandleader and theorist [George Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(composer) "George Russell (composer)"). In 1958, Evans joined [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s sextet, which in 1959, then immersed in [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), recorded _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_, the best-selling jazz album of all time.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-:0-3) In late 1959, Evans left Davis's band and began his career as a leader, forming a [trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_trio "Jazz trio") with bassist [Scott LaFaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_LaFaro "Scott LaFaro") and drummer [Paul Motian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Motian "Paul Motian"), a group now regarded as a seminal modern jazz trio. They recorded two studio albums, _[Portrait in Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_in_Jazz "Portrait in Jazz")_ and _[Explorations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorations_(Bill_Evans_album) "Explorations (Bill Evans album)")_, and two albums recorded during a 1961 engagement at New York's [Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Village_Vanguard "Village Vanguard") jazz club: _[Sunday at the Village Vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday_at_the_Village_Vanguard "Sunday at the Village Vanguard")_ and _[Waltz for Debby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz_for_Debby_(1962_album) "Waltz for Debby (1962 album)")_. A complete set (on three CDs) of their Vanguard recordings was issued decades later. Ten days after this booking ended, LaFaro died in a car crash. After months without public performances, Evans reemerged with a new trio featuring [Chuck Israels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Israels "Chuck Israels") on bass. In 1963, Evans recorded the [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award")–winning _[Conversations with Myself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversations_with_Myself_(album) "Conversations with Myself (album)")_, a solo album produced with [overdubbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdubbing "Overdubbing") technology. In 1966, he met bassist [Eddie Gómez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_G%C3%B3mez_(musician) "Eddie Gómez (musician)"), with whom he worked for the next 11 years. In the mid-1970s, Evans collaborated with the singer [Tony Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bennett "Tony Bennett") on two critically acclaimed albums: _[The Tony Bennett/Bill Evans Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Bennett/Bill_Evans_Album "The Tony Bennett/Bill Evans Album")_ (1975) and _[Together Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Together_Again_(Tony_Bennett_and_Bill_Evans_album) "Together Again (Tony Bennett and Bill Evans album)")_ (1977). Many of Evans's compositions, such as " [Waltz for Debby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz_for_Debby_(song) "Waltz for Debby (song)")" and " [Time Remembered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Remembered "Time Remembered")", have become [standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"), played and recorded by many artists. Evans received 31 Grammy nominations and seven awards, and was inducted into the [_DownBeat_ Jazz Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans#cite_note-4) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] -
